lessons.title: 10.1 Introduction: what is a computer network?

blocks.html: A computer network is a group of two or more computers and other devices (printers, phones, servers) connected together so that they can share data and resources. Each device on a network is called a node or host.

items.html: Resource sharing: a whole computer lab can print on one printer.
Communication: email, WhatsApp, video classes.
Data sharing: the school office and the principal see the same student records (Chapter 8).
Central storage and backup: files stay safe on a server or in the cloud.
Cost saving: one Internet connection serves many users.

blocks.html: Networks around you: the school computer lab, your home Wi-Fi, the mobile phone network, a bank's ATM network, the railway reservation system, and the Internet itself.

rows: ARPANET is started by the US Department of Defense and links four university computers. It is the first packet-switched network.
The first email is sent over ARPANET (Ray Tomlinson; the @ sign is chosen).
ARPANET switches to the TCP/IP protocols, the start of the modern Internet.
NSFNET connects universities in the US and grows into the Internet backbone.
Tim Berners-Lee at CERN creates the World Wide Web (HTML, HTTP, URLs).
Public Internet service starts in India (VSNL, 15 August 1995).
Broadband, Wi-Fi and 3G mobile Internet spread.
4G, smartphones, cloud computing and UPI change daily life in India.
5G launches in India (October 2022); Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7 bring faster wireless networks; billions of IoT devices go online.

blocks.html: The topology of a network is the way its nodes are arranged and connected.

rows: All nodes are connected to one main cable (the backbone), with terminators at both ends
Cheap; little cable; easy to add a node
If the backbone breaks, the whole network fails; slow when traffic is heavy; faults are hard to find
Every node is connected to a central hub or switch
Easy to install and manage; one faulty cable affects only one node; easy to find faults
If the central device fails, the whole network stops; needs more cable
Each node is connected to two neighbours, forming a circle; data travels in one direction
No collisions; equal access for all nodes
One broken node or link can stop the ring; adding nodes disturbs the network
Every node is connected to many (or all) other nodes
Very reliable: if one link fails, data takes another path; secure
Very expensive; needs a lot of cable; hard to set up
Star networks connected to a main backbone in levels
Easy to expand; suits large organisations; a fault stays in one branch
If the backbone or a top-level node fails, its branches are cut off

blocks.caption: Figure 10.2 · network topologies (circles = computers, squares = hub or switch)

blocks.html: For a full mesh of n nodes, the number of links is n(n − 1) / 2. For 5 nodes that is 10 links, and for 10 nodes it is 45.

items.html: School computer lab: star (simple, easy to fix).
A school with several labs on different floors: tree (a star in each lab, linked to a main switch).
Bank data centres and the Internet backbone: mesh (reliability is most important).

blocks.html: Just as every house has an address so that letters reach it, every node on a network needs an address.

items.html: A 48-bit (6-byte) number burnt into the NIC by its manufacturer. It is written as 6 pairs of hexadecimal digits: 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E .
The first 3 bytes identify the manufacturer, and the last 3 bytes are the card's own serial number.
It is meant to be permanent and unique, and is used inside a LAN (switches use it).
Given to a device by the network, and it can change. For example, your phone gets a new IP address on school Wi-Fi.
Used to deliver data between networks, across the Internet (routers use it).
IPv4: 32 bits, written as 4 numbers (octets) from 0 to 255 separated by dots:

blocks.html: 192.168.1.10 . That gives 2³², about 430 crore (4.3 billion) addresses, which is no
longer enough.

items.html: IPv6: 128 bits, written as 8 groups of hexadecimal digits:

blocks.html: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 . It gives so many addresses that every
device on Earth can have its own.
IPv4 address classes (decided by the first octet)
In Chapter 9, tcp://127.0.0.1:3306 meant "the MySQL server on this computer, at port 3306".

lessons.title: 10.7 The Internet, the WWW, DNS and URLs

rows: A worldwide network of networks (the hardware and the connections)
A service that runs on the Internet: a huge collection of linked web pages
Carries email, video calls, file transfer, online games, and the Web
Uses HTML pages, HTTP/HTTPS and URLs

blocks.html: Think of the Internet as the roads and the Web as one kind of vehicle that uses them.

Web terms: a web page is one HTML document. A website is a group of related web pages under one domain. A web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) shows web pages. A web server stores websites and sends pages when asked.
People remember names, but computers use IP addresses. A domain name such as
www.example.in is the friendly name of a server.
A domain name is read from right to left:

items.html: .in is the top-level domain (TLD): a country code for India. Other TLDs are .com , .org , .edu , .gov and .uk .
example is the second-level domain, the name the owner registers.
www is the host or subdomain.

blocks.html: The Domain Name System (DNS) is the Internet's phone book. It turns a domain name into an IP address.

blocks.text: What happens when you type a website's name

items.html: The browser checks its own cache for the IP address.
If the address is not there, it asks a DNS resolver, usually run by your Internet

blocks.html: provider.

items.html: The resolver asks the root server, then the TLD server (for .in ), then the domain's

blocks.html: authoritative server.

items.html: The IP address comes back, and the browser connects to the web server at that IP.
The server sends the web page, and the browser displays it.

blocks.caption: Figure 10.3 · a DNS lookup, step by step

blocks.html: All of this usually takes only a fraction of a second.

blocks.text: Example 1: Case study, designing a school campus network

blocks.html: Gyan Vidya School, Patna has four blocks. The distances between blocks and the number of computers in each block are given below.

(a) Where should the server be placed? In the Science block, because it has the most computers (80). Most of the traffic then stays inside one building. (The rule of thumb is to put the server where the most computers are.)
(b) Suggest a cable layout. A star with the Science block at the centre: Science–Admin (60 m), Science–Junior (70 m) and Science–Library (80 m), a total of 210 m. Every link is shorter than 100 m.
(c) Which device is needed inside each block? A switch, to connect all the computers of that block.

(d) Where is a repeater needed? In the suggested layout, nowhere, because every link is under 100 m, the normal limit for a twisted-pair Ethernet run. If Admin were linked directly to Junior (120 m), a repeater would be needed on that link.

(e) What type of network is the campus network? A LAN. If the school links it to its head office in Delhi, that link is a WAN, through an Internet provider or a leased line, with a router at the school.

items.html: A computer network connects devices (nodes) to share data and resources.
Networking began with ARPANET (1969). TCP/IP (1983) and NSFNET built the Internet. Tim Berners-Lee created the WWW (1989–91). India got public Internet in 1995 and 5G in 2022.
Network types by area: PAN (personal), LAN (building or campus), MAN (city), WAN (country or world). The Internet is the largest WAN.

Devices: modem (digital ↔ analog), NIC (has the MAC address), RJ45 (Ethernet plug), repeater (boosts the signal), hub (sends to all ports), switch (sends to one port, uses MAC), router (joins networks, uses IP), gateway (joins different protocols), access point (Wi-Fi).
Topologies: bus, star, ring, mesh (n(n − 1)/2 links) and tree.
MAC = 48-bit permanent hardware address. IP = logical address: IPv4 has 32 bits, IPv6 has 128 bits.
The Internet is the network. The WWW is a service on it. DNS turns domain names into IP addresses. A URL = protocol + domain + path + query.
